questions.question: Why must `error.tsx` always be a Client Component?
options: It's an arbitrary restriction that may change
Error boundaries rely on class-component-style lifecycle behavior, which only works client-side
It needs access to browser localStorage
questions.explanation: React error boundaries are implemented using lifecycle methods that only exist in the client rendering model, so `error.tsx` requires the "use client" directive.

questions.question: Why can't a regular `error.tsx` catch an error thrown inside the root `layout.tsx`?
options: Because the layout wraps the error boundary itself, so the boundary can't catch an error from its own ancestor — `global-error.tsx` is needed instead
It's a bug that will be fixed in a future version
questions.explanation: The error boundary created by `error.tsx` sits inside the layout, so it cannot catch a failure in the layout that wraps it — `global-error.tsx` handles that case by replacing the whole root layout.

questions.question: What does calling `notFound()` inside a Server Component page do?
options: Throws an unrecoverable error that crashes the server
Renders the nearest not-found.tsx (or the built-in default) with a proper 404 status code
Only works in Route Handlers, not pages
questions.explanation: `notFound()` is the App Router's mechanism for rendering a 404 state with the correct status code, used in this app whenever a course or lesson slug doesn't exist.

questions.question: For an expected failure inside a Server Action, like invalid form input, what's the recommended approach?
options: Always throw, so the nearest error.tsx handles it
Catch it and return a plain error value the calling component can render inline, reserving throw for truly unrecoverable failures
Log it silently and do nothing
Redirect to a generic error page every time
questions.explanation: Throwing triggers the heavy-handed error boundary UI; returning an error object lets the form show a normal inline validation message instead.
